definition: The second-stage model in modern retrieval: take the top 50-200 candidates from fast first-stage retrieval and reorder them with a cross-encoder (or LLM judge).
details: The second-stage model in modern retrieval: take the top 50-200 candidates from fast first-stage retrieval and reorder them with a cross-encoder (or LLM judge). Usually the single highest-ROI upgrade to RAG quality.

explainer.lead: It is the second stage of modern retrieval, taking the top candidates from fast retrieval and reordering them with a stronger model. It matters because it is usually the single highest-return upgrade to retrieval-augmented generation quality.

tiers.eli5: A quick librarian pulls a rough pile of books, then an expert reads the pile and puts the best ones on top.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers feed the top 50 to 200 first-stage hits to a cross-encoder or LLM judge for reordering. A pitfall is latency and cost: the stronger model only sees what the first stage surfaced, so a missed document cannot be recovered.
tiers.paperLevel: A function scoring each query-document pair jointly, applied to the top-k candidate set from a fast first-stage retriever, producing a reordered list. Its quality ceiling is set by first-stage recall and its cost grows with the number of candidates scored.

explainer.example: A vector search returns 100 passages; a cross-encoder scores each against the question and moves the truly relevant passage from rank 40 to rank 1.
